content: The classification of income groups in this report is based on the World Bank's list of economies as of July 2014. For the Cook Islands, Nauru, and Niue, income group classification was determined using gross domestic product (GDP). Among the 62 countries analyzed, 21 reported over 90% of their national blood collections, while eight countries reported less than 50%. To create a global overview, percentages were used to calculate adjusted figures for total collections and donations per 1,000 population. In some cases, countries provided coverage percentages without a sampling frame or basis, necessitating decisions on whether to apply estimated percentages to adjust total collections and donation rates. Partial data were sometimes assumed to represent the entire country, though this may present a more favorable picture than reality, especially in lowand middle-income countries where data often reflect major cities with better facilities and wider coverage, leaving rural areas underrepresented. Caution is advised against generalizing these data. Updated indicators in this report may differ slightly from those in the WHO Fact Sheet 279 on blood safety and availability (updated July 2016) and regional reports due to differences in data availability and adjustments following validation. A higher proportion of middleand low-income countries reported only reactive results for transfusion-transmissible infection testing, without confirmatory test results. Countries that did not provide confirmatory test results may have higher percentages of positive results among donations. Testing strategies and protocols vary between countries; in some, a sample was considered positive if it was repeatedly reactive twice, without additional confirmatory tests. The report includes data from various countries and years, highlighting the number of blood centers, their coverage, and the percentage of national blood collections they represent. For example, in Argentina, 16 out of 55 blood centers were covered, accounting for 29% of the country's blood collections. In Egypt, the data reflect the National Blood Transfusion Services, which operates 24 regional blood banks covering most governorates, excluding 6% of collections from hospital-based blood banks. In Kenya, the Kenya National Blood Transfusion Service (KNBTS) collected 158,000 units of blood, representing approximately 50% of the national requirement. In some countries, data from private or hospital-based blood banks were not included in the report. For instance, in China, data from one hospital-based blood center were excluded. Similarly, in Turkey, annual data from hospital-based transfusion centers were not included, though the total number of blood and component collections in 2011 was 2,182,394 units. In South Africa, blood services are delivered by two independent organizations, SANBS and WPBTS, and the report provides a national summary of their activities. The report also notes challenges in data collection, such as incomplete reporting from private hospitals, inaccessible areas due to insecurity, and the exclusion of military and police hospital collections in some countries. For example, in Somalia, parts of the country were inaccessible, and data from transfusion centers in those areas were not received. In South Sudan, data from two hospitals accounted for approximately 75% of the estimated national total. In summary, this report provides a comprehensive overview of blood collection and donation data across various countries, highlighting disparities in reporting, coverage, and testing protocols. It emphasizes the need for caution in interpreting and generalizing the data, particularly for lowand middle-income countries where rural areas may be underrepresented.
